idiom_name: var prop: T by Delegates.observable(initial) { prop, old, new -> ... }
implementation_notes: kotlin-stdlib ships the single-subject form of the pattern: `var price: Double by Delegates.observable(0.0) { prop, old, new -> ... }` runs the handler after every assignment (vetoable() runs before it and can reject the new value). It replaces the Subject/Observer pair for property-level notification, but holds exactly one handler per property - several subscribers need an explicit MutableList<(T) -> Unit> or a shared flow. Property delegation is compiler sugar, so the handler receives a KProperty instead of an Observer interface.
pitfalls: The delegate stores its handler for the property's lifetime and notifies exactly one: multiple subscribers require your own list (or a flow), and the handler cannot be unregistered.
The handler runs inline on the assigning thread: re-entrant assignment inside it recurses, and UI updates from a background assignment must be re-dispatched.
A plain MutableList of listeners is a strong-reference registry: removal has to be explicit or the list needs weak-reference wrappers, or listeners outlive their owner.
Delegates.observable fires even when the assigned value is unchanged; guard with old != new when that matters (vetoable() cannot guard equality, only validity).

variants.name: MutableSharedFlow (coroutines, hot broadcast stream)
variants.idiom_name: MutableSharedFlow<Event> with collect{} subscribers and tryEmit/emit
variants.implementation_notes: The coroutine realization is a hot shared flow: any number of collectors subscribe with collect{} (a suspend function), emit() suspends when the buffer is full (or tryEmit() drops), subscriptionCount reports active collectors, and every method is documented thread-safe. It replaces the registry plus locks with structured concurrency: unsubscription is cancelling the collecting job, and backpressure comes from replay/extraBufferCapacity/onBufferOverflow instead of an unbounded callback list. Use it when notifications cross coroutines; Delegates.observable remains right for one local property.
pitfalls: emit() suspends on a full buffer, so a slow collector can block the publisher; tryEmit() drops instead and DROP_OLDEST discards events for every subscriber, not just the slow one.
A SharedFlow without replay delivers only events emitted after the collector starts - subscribing is not a snapshot of current state (use StateFlow for that).
Subscriptions live as long as their collecting coroutine: a collector launched in a global scope outlives its owner and must be cancelled explicitly (viewModelScope/lifecycleScope exist for this).
Collectors resume on their own dispatcher: emitting from a background thread does not move handler work to the main thread.
